title: Pod to pod across nodes
summary: The network model delivers a packet without NAT.

steps.n: Pod A sends a packet to the IP address of pod B.
The node routing table says that range belongs to node 2.
The packet travels over the node network, encapsulated or routed depending on the plugin.
Node 2 receives the packet and finds the local interface for pod B.
The packet reaches pod B with the original source address intact.
Pod B answers along the same path and pod A sees the real pod IP.

title: What the CNI does at pod start
summary: The plugin builds a network for a new pod.

steps.n: The kubelet asks the runtime to create the pod sandbox.
The runtime calls the CNI plugin with the pod name and namespace.
The plugin creates a virtual ethernet pair and puts one end in the pod namespace.
It takes an address from the node range and records it.
Routes or tunnel rules are added so other nodes can reach the pod.
The runtime starts the containers, which already have network.

title: Failure and recovery: an MTU mismatch
summary: Small packets work and large ones hang until MTU is corrected.

steps.n: Small pings between pods on different nodes succeed.
A download starts and then stalls because full size packets are dropped.
The overlay adds extra header bytes so a full packet exceeds the node link size.
The operator compares the overlay and node interface sizes and finds them equal.
They set the overlay MTU below the node MTU by the header size.
Large transfers complete between the pods.
The value is added to the install configuration so new nodes use it.

title: How a Service address reaches a pod

steps.n: The client sends traffic to the ClusterIP and port of the Service.
On the client node, kube-proxy rules match that destination.
One ready pod address is chosen from the Service endpoints.
The destination is changed to the chosen pod IP and port.
The pod replies and the node rewrites the source back to the Service IP.
The client never learns which pod answered.

title: Failure and recovery: the empty Service
summary: A label mismatch leaves a Service with no endpoints.

steps.n: Requests to the Service hang and then fail.
The developer sees the selector app equals web.
The endpoint list is empty, so no backend exists.
The pods are labelled app equals webapp, so they do not match.
The Service selector is corrected to app equals webapp.
The controller adds the ready pod addresses to the endpoint slice.
Traffic reaches the pods and a check for empty endpoints is added to the alerts.

title: Rolling update and endpoints
summary: Endpoints follow readiness during a rollout.

steps.n: The Deployment starts a new pod with the new version.
The pod is not added to endpoints until its readiness probe passes.
Once ready, its address appears in the endpoint slice.
The Deployment marks an old pod as terminating.
The address is removed from the slice and clients stop receiving new requests.
The old pod finishes current requests during its grace period before it exits.

title: A name lookup in a pod
summary: The resolver walks the search list.

steps.n: The app asks the resolver for the short name api.
The resolver asks for api.prod.svc.cluster.local first.
CoreDNS finds the Service from its cache of the API.
CoreDNS returns the ClusterIP and the resolver gives it to the app.
Later the app asks for api.example.com, which has two dots.
Search domains fail first, then the query is sent upstream and answered.

title: Failure and recovery: DNS overloaded
summary: Lookups time out until CoreDNS is scaled and cached.

steps.n: A busy release multiplies lookups and every name is tried with five search suffixes.
CoreDNS pods reach their CPU limit and some queries are dropped.
Apps log five second DNS timeouts and slow requests.
Dashboards show high DNS latency and requests per second.
They add replicas and raise the CPU limit.
NodeLocal DNSCache is installed so repeated lookups are answered on the node.
Apps use fully qualified names with a trailing dot for external calls.

title: Building a default deny
summary: Deny first, then allow each flow.

steps.n: A policy selects all pods and allows no ingress or egress.
The frontend can no longer reach the backend.
A policy permits ingress to backend on its port from the frontend label only.
The frontend cannot resolve the backend name because egress is denied.
Egress to port 53 of the cluster DNS pods is allowed.
The allowed flow works and a flow from another namespace is still denied.

title: A request through a gateway
summary: Host and path decide the backend.

steps.n: A client sends a request for shop.example.com with path /cart.
The gateway terminates TLS using the certificate on its listener.
The route matching that host and path prefix is selected.
The route sends the request to the cart Service.
The cart Service answers and the gateway returns the response.
A request for /search matches a second route and goes to a different Service.

title: Debugging in a fixed order
summary: Work down from the symptom, one hop at a time.

steps.n: The operator resolves the Service name from a pod and gets an address.
Curl to the ClusterIP times out.
The endpoints list has two ready addresses, so selection is fine.
Curl to one pod IP works, so the application listens correctly.
kube-proxy rules on the client node are missing for this Service.
Restarting kube-proxy on that node recreates the rules and the Service works.

title: Failure and recovery: conntrack table full
summary: Random connection failures end when the table is raised.

steps.n: Some requests fail while others succeed through the same Service.
The node kernel log says the conntrack table is full and packets are dropped.
The operator finds the messages at the time of the failures.
Counting entries shows the limit is reached by many short DNS connections.
They raise the conntrack maximum on the nodes.
They enable NodeLocal DNSCache to cut short lived connections.
Requests succeed consistently and an alert watches conntrack usage.
